messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
Completeness implies the condition because choosing x_n \in F_n for each n makes (x_n) Cauchy when the diameters tend to zero, and its limit x belongs to every F_n, giving a nonempty intersection.
The reverse implication follows because, for any Cauchy sequence (x_n), the sets F_k = \overline{\{x_m: m\ge k\}} are nonempty, closed, nested, and have diameters tending to zero, so their intersection contains a point x that is a limit of x_n.
Does this prove the equivalence?
